68. Incubator Baby Exhibit

In 1897, Coney Island welcomed an unusual attraction: Dr. Martin Couney and his Incubator Baby Exhibit, where visitors paid ten cents to view premature infants alongside carnival curiosities. By 1903, Couney established his Infantorium in a repurposed apartment building within the Wonderland amusement park in Minneapolis. At a time when one in five infants perished and 75% of premature babies did not survive their first year, these infants were displayed like museum artifacts, challenging societal norms and medical indifference.

In Europe, incubators were an accepted tool for nurturing premature infants, yet American medical professionals dismissed their value. Steeped in eugenics ideology, many believed premature babies were inherently weak and that their survival would perpetuate undesirable traits. Allowing these infants to die, they argued, strengthened the human race by ensuring only the fittest survived. Couney, a German Jewish immigrant who, notably, lacked a medical license, rejected this view. Inspired by European practices, he sought to save these vulnerable lives through innovative care.

At the Infantorium, Couney employed trained nurses, ensured infants received breast milk, and maintained temperature-controlled incubators with filtered air. Parents, often referred to Couney by doctors as a last resort, entrusted their babies to his care at no cost to them. The operation, funded by a 25-cent admission fee and thousands of visitors, supported daily expenses of $15 per infant and provided nurses with decent wages. Upon arrival, infants received a warm bath, a dose of brandy and a coloured identification wristband. Strict adherence to hygiene protocols and medical procedures enforced by a head nurse who later married Couney, underscored the professionalism of the operation. Their own premature daughter, saved by the high standards of care and an incubator, grew up to become a nurse and contributed to the cause.

The exhibit gained prominence at world fairs, showcasing industrial, technological and cultural advancements. At the 1898 Omaha World Fair, his strategic marketing drew widespread attention, funding a lavish lifestyle that included a grand home and extravagant parties. Yet, Couney died penniless, having invested his wealth in this mission. The 1901 Buffalo World’s Fair, overshadowed  by the assassination of President McKinley, saw nurses presenting incubator babies to captivated audiences, tugging at visitor emotions and wallets. Inspired by chicken hatcheries, viewing windows allowed spectators to follow the progress of their favourite infants, a practice that, while lifesaving, bordered on a macabre spectacle.

Public fascination was evident in media coverage. Despite the national tragedy of a presidential death, newspapers fixated on the incubator babies. An anonymous editorial critiquing the eugenics-leaning medical establishment sparked debate, highlighting ethical tensions. It was not until 1938, during the Great Depression, that Dr. Julius Hess collaborated with Couney to establish formal medical incubator facilities. Statistics revealed that infants in incubators were four times more likely to survive, and over 45 years, Couney saved 6,500+ lives. A one-year reunion of surviving infants in the early 1940s served as a powerful public relations event, paving the way for the first dedicated premature infant department in a New York hospital in 1943.

The ethics of displaying infants remain contentious. The work of Couney, while humanitarian, profited from public curiosity, raising questions about exploitation. Some draw speculative connections to the orphan train movement, the rise in asylum admissions and theories involving 'cabbage patch babies', 'cloning' or a 'Tartarian reset.' Was the Infantorium a noble endeavour that saved thousands, or did its commercial spectacle conceal a darker motive? What do you think?
